bib.title: MemoryArena: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks" (MemoryArena). Zexue He, Yu Wang, Churan Zhi, Yuanzhe Hu, Tzu-Ping Chen, Lang Yin, Ze Chen, Tong Arthur Wu, Siru Ouyang, Zihan Wang, Jiaxin Pei, Julian McAuley, Yejin Choi, Alex Pentland. Venue as printed on p1: "Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026." arXiv:2602.16313v2, stamped 17 Sep 2026.

COVERAGE: 31 of 31 pages, all 116,398 extracted chars: main text p1-9, impact/limitations p10, references p10-11 (skimmed), appendices A-C p12-31 (read, including Tables 5-8 and the case studies). Figure 3 plot values did not extract, so I only have its caption and the prose about it.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: The paper asserts that systems near-saturated on recall benchmarks do poorly here, but it reports no LoCoMo or LongMemEval scores of its own, so the recall-versus-task gap is asserted, not measured side by side.
  number: none
  setup: abstract and intro framing only
  quote: "agents with near-saturated performance on existing long-context memory benchmarks like LoCoMo perform poorly in our agentic setting"
  where: p1

- claim: The stated difference from LoCoMo/LongMemEval is that those test post hoc recall with a single query over a fixed history, with no actions or environment feedback.
  number: none
  setup: Table 1 marks LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench and MemoryBench as having no agentic actions, no environment feedback and no interdependent subtasks
  quote: "these benchmarks primarily evaluate static memorization through post hoc recall using a single query and do not involve an agentic or interactive environment in which memory must be actively used"
  where: p3

- claim: Task success is near zero to low everywhere, while per-subtask progress is much higher.
  number: all-method average SR/PS: shopping 0.02/0.52, travel 0.00/0.02 (sPS 0.38), web search 0.23/0.09, math 0.18/0.29, physics 0.42/0.56
  setup: GPT-5-mini as task agent (Table 3 labels it GPT-5.1-mini); 4 long-context models, 5 memory systems, 4 RAG systems; memory retrieved once per session
  quote: "All Method Avg0.02 0.52 0.00 0.02 0.38 0.23 0.09 0.18 0.29 0.42 0.56"
  where: p7, Table 3

- claim: Sessions depend on each other by construction: later subtasks are underspecified without earlier state, and causal order is enforced.
  number: 701 tasks, 6.9 interdependent subtasks per task on average, 57 action steps, 4,850 subtasks in total; travel dependency chains up to depth four
  setup: shopping 150 (6 sessions, compatibility chains), group travel 270 (5-9 sessions, JOIN and RELATION constraints on earlier travellers), progressive web search 221 (2-16), math 40 and physics 20 (lemma chains)
  quote: "later actions are underspecified unless agents correctly track task-relevant information from prior sessions" (p2); "MEMORYARENA✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓701 6.9 57" (p2, Table 1)
  where: p2, p3 Table 2, p5, p10

- claim: Grading is outcome-based with three metrics. SR is the share of tasks fully solved, PS is the fraction of subtasks passed, and sPS is the fraction of constraints satisfied.
  number: none
  setup: shopping and travel need the whole bundle or plan to be right; search and formal reasoning are graded on the final subtask only
  quote: "In Progressive Web Search and Formal Reasoning, success is determined by the correctness of the final subtask"
  where: p7, Sec. 4.2

- claim: External memory and RAG do not reliably beat plain long context.
  number: all-task average SR: long context 0.09-0.19, memory agents 0.12-0.14, RAG 0.17-0.20
  setup: same as Table 3. Memory helps in web search (traces over 120k tokens) and formal reasoning
  quote: "augmenting GPT-5-mini with external memory or RAG does not consistently outperform using the model's full long-context history alone"
  where: p8

- claim: Pass rate falls with dependency distance even when all history is in context.
  number: 0.48, 0.29, 0.21, 0.18, 0.15 for L0-L4
  setup: long-context agent, group travel only; conditional on earlier constraints being correct
  quote: "long-context 0.48 0.29 0.21 0.18 0.15"
  where: p22, Table 7

- claim: Approximate oracle memory (gold prior outcomes plus distilled workflows) lifts success only slightly.
  number: +0.016 shopping, +0.050 travel, +0.05 search, +0.16 math
  setup: long-context setting; the authors call the oracle an approximation
  quote: "∆+0.016 +0.050 +0.05 +0.16"
  where: p22, Table 8

- claim: Success at subtask depth k decays for every method.
  number: none (plot values unreadable)
  setup: Figure 3, four environments
  quote: "all evaluated methods exhibit a decay with no method maintaining a consistent flat region across environments"
  where: p8

- claim: Memory systems cost the most latency per subtask.
  number: GPT-5-mini long context 74.2 s average, Letta 132.8 s, BM25 107.4 s
  setup: per-subtask seconds, averaged over five environments
  quote: "Letta 219 150 121 77 97 132.8"
  where: p9, Table 4

- claim: Results hold in direction with a stronger task agent.
  number: Claude Sonnet 4.6 long-context SR: shopping 0.13, travel 0.00, search 0.06, math 0.37
  setup: only 4 memory configurations rerun
  quote: "Claude-Sonnet-4.6 0.13 0.79 0.00 0.20 0.89 0.06 0.05 0.37 0.4 0.4 0.53"
  where: p21, Table 5

LIMITS
- No recall-benchmark scores for the same systems, so no correlation or paired gap can be cited from this paper.
- How an individual answer is judged correct (exact match, LLM judge, expert) is not stated for search or formal reasoning. No judge validation is reported.
- No confidence intervals, seeds or repeat runs. Math has 40 tasks and physics 20, so physics SR moves in steps of 0.05.
- Outcome grading only; no trajectory scoring. The authors concede they do not isolate individual memory operations: "A finer-grained analysis of individual memory operations across different systems would provide deeper diagnostic insights" (p10).
- Mostly one mid-tier task agent; memory was retrieved once per session, not per action (p17).
- Search SR exceeds PS for many rows, because SR looks only at the final subquery. SR and PS are therefore not comparable across environments.
- Tasks derive from WebShop, TravelPlanner and BrowseComp-Plus; search decomposition was LLM-generated then human-checked.
- Model names and system versions will date.

BUILDS ON: WebShop (Yao et al., 2022); TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024); BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025); experimental setup after LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) and Hu et al. (2025b, MemoryAgentBench); 0D/1D/2D memory taxonomy "Inspired by Hu et al. (2025a)"; contrasted with LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and Evo-Memory (Wei et al., 2025b).

CODE: none worth keeping. The loop is stated as equations 2-4 on p6: retrieve, act on a memory-conditioned policy, then "M ←UPDATE(M,(oi,1:T , ai,1:T ))" after each subtask.

FIGURES: Figure 2, p4, "MEMORYARENA supports four distinct evaluation environments, where a memory-augmented task agent completes a sequence of interdependent subtasks." It shows concretely how session 2 depends on session 1 (the lens must fit the camera body bought earlier), which is faster than prose. Figure 3 (p6, SR at depth k) is the alternative if a results plot is wanted.

PROBLEMS
- Figure 3 axis values and data are garbled in extraction; no depth-k numbers can be quoted.
- Internal inconsistencies in the source: the task agent is "GPT-5-mini" in the text and "GPT-5.1-mini" in the tables; the all-method web search SR of 0.23 is higher than all three group averages (0.04, 0.15, 0.19); Table 8's "original" math value of 0.26 does not match Table 3's 0.21; Table 2 lists web search average trace length as 122.4k while the intro says "more than 40k tokens".
- Math in the formal-reasoning examples (p15, p30-31) extracted poorly; not needed for the claims.
- The appendices contain benchmark prompts written as instructions ("You are an intelligent Shopping Agent...", decomposition prompt p21). They are study materials, not directed at the reader, and I treated them as data.
